This idiom was born in the world of hunting.

Centuries ago, hunting was governed by strict laws. Hunters could only hunt certain animals during certain seasons. Animals that were legally permitted to be hunted were called "game," and if they could be hunted within the rules, they were called "fair game." An animal that was out of season or protected by law was not fair game — chasing it would be wrong and illegal.

Over time, people took this idea out of the forest and into everyday life. They started using it to mean: "This is something I am allowed to go after — the rules permit it."
How It Works in Real Life

The idiom is used across many different situations, but the logic is always the same: something or someone can be legitimately targeted, and no one can complain about it being unfair.

1. Criticism and Public Figures

The most common use. When a person voluntarily steps into public life — a politician, a celebrity, a CEO — their public actions become fair game. Anyone can criticize, analyze, or joke about those actions, and the person cannot reasonably object.

"The senator voted for that bill, so his record on the issue is fair game for reporters to question."

"She chose to be a public figure. Her business decisions are fair game."

Notice: the criticism is earned or justified by their public role. It's not random or unfair.

2. Debate and Discussion

A topic that is fair game is one that is open and acceptable to discuss or debate, without it being considered rude, off-limits, or taboo in that setting.

"In this philosophy class, every idea — no matter how controversial — is fair game for debate."

"Once you publish your book, your writing style is fair game for literary critics."

3. Competition and Strategy

In competitions, a fair game move or target is one that the rules of the game allow.

"In chess, leaving your queen unprotected makes it fair game for your opponent to capture."

"That company undercut our prices — it's a tough move, but it's fair game in business."

4. Romantic Pursuit

When someone is single and available, they are sometimes described as fair game — meaning others may pursue them romantically, and there is nothing wrong with doing so.

"He and his girlfriend broke up last month. I heard he's fair game now."

5. Humor and Teasing

Among friends or in comedy, certain people or topics are fair game for jokes — meaning everyone has agreed (directly or by unspoken understanding) that joking about that thing is acceptable.

"In our friend group, our terrible fashion choices in high school are always fair game."
The Key Idea Hidden Inside the Idiom

What makes "fair game" interesting and important is that it always implies a set of rules or boundaries. Something being "fair game" means it falls within those boundaries. The phrase is meaningful precisely because some things are not fair game.

For example:

  • A politician's voting record → fair game (public behavior, open to scrutiny).
  • That same politician's young child → not fair game (private, not a public figure, deserves protection).

Or:

  • A celebrity's movie performances → fair game (that's their public work).
  • That same celebrity's private medical records → not fair game (private life, crossing a line).

This is why the word "fair" matters so much. It signals that the targeting is justified, not just possible. You could attack someone's private life, but it wouldn't be fair. It's only "fair game" when there's a reason — a rule, a social norm, a context — that makes it acceptable.

"Fair game" is a neutral-to-slightly-assertive phrase. It is often used when someone is defending the right to criticize or pursue something, especially when someone else has objected.

"You can't complain that I questioned your logic — when you make an argument in public, it's fair game."

It can also be used more casually and lightly, without any confrontation:

"Leftover cake in the office kitchen is fair game. Help yourself!"

The idiom is usually used in these patterns:

  • "X is fair game." → The most common form.
  • "X is fair game for Y." → Specifies who is doing the targeting and why.
  • "Consider X fair game." → An opinion about what should be allowed.
  • "Declare/make X fair game." → Announce that something is now open to targeting.

Examples:

  • "His past statements are fair game."
  • "Her work is fair game for peer review."
  • "I consider the whole topic fair game for this discussion."
  • "The leaked documents made the company's finances fair game for investigators."
What the Idiom Does NOT Mean

A few things to be careful about:

  • It does not mean something is fun or easy to go after. It only means it is permitted.
  • It does not mean that all methods of going after something are acceptable — just that the target itself is acceptable.
  • It is not the same as "fair play," which refers to behaving honestly and by the rules during a competition. "Fair game" is about whether the target is legitimate; "fair play" is about whether your methods are honest.

ConceptExplanation

"Fair game" means a person, topic, or thing that is a legitimate, acceptable, and justified target — for criticism, humor, pursuit, investigation, or action. The phrase comes from hunting, where it referred to animals that could legally be hunted. Today, it is used figuratively in everyday speech to signal that going after something is within the rules — social, ethical, or otherwise. Its power comes from the contrast: not everything is fair game, and calling something "fair game" is a way of saying "this one is — and no one can fairly object."
5845:
A fair-weather friend is someone who is friendly, supportive, and pleasant to be around only when things are going well for you — but who disappears, pulls away, or even turns against you the moment you face trouble, hardship, or difficulty.

In short: they are your friend only when it is easy and convenient to be your friend.

The phrase is borrowed directly from the world of weather and sailing.

In the old days of sailing ships, certain sailors or crew members would only agree to sail when the weather was calm and the skies were clear — the so-called "fair weather." The moment a storm appeared on the horizon, they would refuse to sail, abandon the ship, or prove completely useless. You could not rely on them when conditions became hard.

Over time, people began using this same idea to describe unreliable people in everyday life. The word "fair" here means pleasant, good, or clear — not fair as in "just" or "equal." So "fair weather" simply means good times, and a "fair-weather friend" is someone who only shows up during those good times.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

• Fair → pleasant, calm, easy (like fair weather = sunny, clear skies)
  • Weather → conditions (used here as a metaphor for life's circumstances)
  • Friend → someone who is supposed to be loyal and caring

Put together: a "friend" who only sticks around during the calm, easy, pleasant conditions of your life.
The Core Idea: What Makes Someone a Fair-Weather Friend?

Here are the key behaviors that define a fair-weather friend:

1. They love you when you're winning.
When you're successful, popular, happy, or doing well, they are right by your side — laughing with you, celebrating with you, enjoying the good times.

2. They vanish when things go wrong.
The moment you lose your job, face an illness, go through a breakup, make a mistake, or fall into hard times, they suddenly become "busy." They stop calling. They make excuses. They are nowhere to be found.

3. They offer no real support.
A true friend helps you carry emotional weight during difficult times. A fair-weather friend is not built for that. Supporting you when it is inconvenient or uncomfortable is simply not something they are willing to do.

4. They may even distance themselves to protect their own image.
Sometimes, a fair-weather friend pulls away not because they don't care, but because being associated with someone who is struggling might make them look bad. They are protecting themselves, not you.

5. They return when things improve.
Interestingly, many fair-weather friends come back once your situation improves. They reappear and act as though nothing happened — because, for them, the good times are back and it is convenient to be around you again.

Here are several examples that show how the idiom is used in real life:

  • "When I had money and a great social life, everyone wanted to hang out with me. But when I lost my job and needed help, nobody showed up. I realized I was surrounded by fair-weather friends."
  • "Don't count on Jake during a crisis — he's a fair-weather friend. He'll celebrate your wins but disappear during your struggles."
  • "She found out who her real friends were during her illness. Most of them were fair-weather friends who couldn't handle the situation."
  • "I thought we were close, but when I really needed someone to talk to, he was unavailable. Classic fair-weather friendship."
The Opposite of a Fair-Weather Friend

The opposite of a fair-weather friend is someone often described as:

  • A true friend / a real friend — someone who is there for you in both good times and bad.
  • A loyal friend — someone whose support does not depend on how well things are going for you.
  • An all-weather friend — a less common but beautifully fitting phrase that means the exact opposite: a friend who stands by you regardless of life's storms.

There is also a well-known saying that captures this contrast perfectly:

"A friend in need is a friend indeed."

This means: the person who shows up when you are truly in need — that is the real friend. A fair-weather friend fails this test completely.

Understanding this idiom is about more than just learning a phrase — it teaches you something important about the nature of friendship itself.

True friendship is tested during hard times, not good times. It is easy to be someone's friend when everything is going smoothly. The real measure of a friend is whether they stay when the storm hits. A fair-weather friend is someone who has never truly passed that test.

Recognizing fair-weather friends in your own life can help you:

  • Invest your time and trust in people who genuinely care about you.
  • Avoid feeling hurt and confused when certain people disappear during your struggles.
  • Appreciate the real friends who do show up, because they are rare and valuable.
Tone and Register: How and When to Use This Idiom

This idiom is informal to semi-formal in tone. It is perfectly appropriate in:

  • Casual conversation with friends or family.
  • Personal writing, journals, or essays.
  • Workplace discussions (e.g., talking about unreliable colleagues or superficial professional relationships).
  • Literature, journalism, and opinion pieces.

It is rarely used in highly formal or technical contexts, but it would not be out of place in a well-written formal essay if used deliberately.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

MeaningA friend who is only around during good times and disappears during hard times
OriginSailing — crew who only sailed in calm, fair weather
Key word"Fair" = pleasant/good (not "fair" as in just or equal)
OppositeA true/loyal/all-weather friend
LessonReal friendship is proven during difficulty, not comfort

If you walk away with one thing, let it be this: a fair-weather friend is sunshine-only. The moment clouds appear in your life, they are gone. A true friend, by contrast, brings an umbrella.
5846: A fairway is a clear, open, designated path or channel — the safe, ideal route through a space that has less-ideal or more dangerous alternatives on either side. This idea plays out in two main areas where the word is used.
1. In Golf — the most common meaning

A golf course is divided into individual units called holes (typically 18 of them). Each hole has three main zones:

  • The tee — where you stand and hit the ball to start the hole.
  • The green — the smooth, closely cut grass at the far end, where the actual cup (hole) is located.
  • And in between these two: the fairway.

The fairway is the wide strip of short, neatly mowed grass that connects the tee to the green. It is the intended landing zone for your shots — the "good" area to be in.

On either side of the fairway, there is usually the rough — longer, thicker, and harder-to-play-from grass — and often hazards like sand bunkers, trees, or water. The fairway is considered favorable because the short grass gives you a clean, solid surface to hit your next shot from. When your ball lands in the rough or a hazard, the game becomes much harder.

So when a golfer says "I hit the fairway," it means they struck the ball well and it landed in that ideal central strip — a good outcome. "I missed the fairway" means the ball drifted into the rough or a hazard.

Fairways differ from hole to hole. Some are wide and forgiving, some are narrow and demanding. Some run straight, while others curve to the left or right — a shape golfers call a dogleg. Fairways also vary in length, from short par-3 holes (which may have almost no fairway at all) to long par-5 holes with sweeping fairways of several hundred meters.

On water, a fairway is a navigable channel — a stretch of water in a river, harbor, bay, or coastline that is deep enough, wide enough, and clear enough for ships and boats to pass through safely.

Imagine a large harbor or a river mouth. The water is not uniformly safe everywhere — some parts may be too shallow, have hidden rocks, or be filled with obstacles. The fairway is the specific, well-defined corridor that vessels follow to enter and exit without running aground or into danger.

In busy ports and harbors, fairways are typically marked with buoys (floating markers) so sailors know exactly where the safe channel lies. On nautical charts (maps used at sea), fairways are clearly drawn in. Maritime law also regulates how vessels behave in a fairway — for example, large ships that cannot easily maneuver often have the right of way in a narrow fairway, and smaller vessels must give way to them.

Whether on a golf course or at sea, a fairway is always:

  • A designated, clear path within a larger space
  • The best or safest route through that space
  • Surrounded on its sides by less ideal or more dangerous territory

The golf fairway is flanked by rough and hazards. The nautical fairway is flanked by shallow water and obstacles. In both cases, staying in the fairway means you are on the right track — in a good, clean, manageable position.

• "His drive landed perfectly in the center of the fairway, leaving him a simple iron shot to the green." — golf
  • "The fairway on the 14th hole curves sharply to the left, making it one of the trickiest on the course." — golf
  • "The tanker slowly made its way through the narrow fairway into the port." — nautical
  • "Small boats are advised to keep to the starboard side of the fairway to allow larger vessels to pass safely." — nautical

"Fairway" is almost always used in one of these two contexts. In golf, it is an everyday term that comes up constantly in commentary, conversation, and writing about the sport. In maritime settings, it is a precise technical and legal term used in navigation, port regulations, and international maritime law.

You will rarely, if ever, see "fairway" used outside these two domains in serious writing. When you do, it's usually a metaphor borrowing the golf sense — meaning a clear, smooth path forward through something — but this is informal and uncommon.
5847:
A fait accompli is something that has already been done — completely finished — before the people affected by it even had a chance to weigh in, object, or influence it. By the time they find out, it's too late. The action is complete, locked in, and reversing it would be extremely difficult or practically impossible.

Think of it as someone saying: "Here's what happened. It's done. Deal with it."
What Makes It a Fait Accompli — and Not Just "A Decision"

This is the crucial distinction. A regular decision can be discussed, debated, voted on, or reversed. A fait accompli deliberately skips all of that. The person who creates it acts first and informs others after, knowing full well that once the action is done, resistance becomes far harder — or pointless.

Three things define it:

1. It's already done.
Not planned. Not proposed. Completed.

2. Others find out only after.
They had no voice in it beforehand — and often, no warning.

3. It's very hard to undo.
This is what gives it its power. The difficulty of reversal is what makes it a strategy, not just an accident.

"Fait accompli" is not a neutral word. It almost always carries a slightly negative or manipulative feeling. When someone creates a fait accompli, there's usually an implication that they deliberately bypassed discussion, consent, or approval — because they knew others might say no, or slow things down.

It's a power move. The person acting acts fast and decisively, presenting the result to everyone else as an unchangeable reality.

That said, it can sometimes be used in a dryly matter-of-fact way — not always with strong judgment — just to acknowledge: this was done before anyone could stop it.

In a workplace:
A CEO signs a deal to merge with another company, then calls a company-wide meeting to "announce the exciting news." The employees never had a say. The deal is signed and sealed. That's a fait accompli.

In a family:
Your parents tell you over dinner that they've already sold the family home and bought a new one in a different city. You find out only now, moving boxes are arriving next week. Done. That's a fait accompli.

In politics:
A government quietly builds a military base in a disputed territory, then informs the international community. Removing it now would be a logistical and political nightmare. They've created a fait accompli — the presence on the ground forces everyone else to respond to a new reality.

In a friendship:
Your friend tells you they've already RSVP'd for both of you to a wedding without asking you first. It would be awkward to cancel now. Small scale — same idea.

People and organizations deliberately create faits accomplis as a tactic. The logic is:

"If I ask first, they might say no. But if I act first and ask forgiveness later — or don't ask at all — the cost of undoing what I've done will discourage any real opposition."

It exploits the simple human tendency to accept existing reality more easily than to fight to reverse it. Reversing something that already exists takes far more effort, money, political will, or emotional energy than stopping it before it happens.
The plural of "fait accompli" is faits accomplis — both words get the "s." You'll see and hear both forms fairly often.

A fait accompli is a completed action — presented to others as a done deal — that was carried out before those people could object, debate, or prevent it, and is now extremely difficult to reverse. It implies a deliberate bypassing of consent or discussion. The power of it lies entirely in the difficulty of undoing what is already done.

Whenever you see or hear this phrase, the underlying message is always the same: the window to stop this has already closed.
5848:
Faith means a strong, confident belief or trust in someone or something — held even when you cannot fully prove it or verify it with your own eyes. It is not just a weak guess or a vague hope. It is a firm, settled conviction that something is true, or that someone is reliable and good.

Think of it this way: when you sit down on a chair, you don't carefully inspect every joint and screw to make sure it will hold your weight. You simply trust that it will. That quiet, confident trust — extended toward people, ideas, or higher powers — is the spirit of faith.

Faith has two sides that always work together: belief and trust.

Belief is the mental part — you are convinced that something is true or real. Trust is the relational, emotional part — you are willing to depend on it or act on it. Faith is never purely cold and intellectual. It always involves a willingness to lean on what you believe in.

This is what separates faith from just "knowing a fact." You might know that a bridge was built in 1990. But if you are afraid to walk across it, you lack faith in it. True faith leads to action or commitment. A person who says they have faith in a friend doesn't just think the friend is decent — they are willing to count on that friend when it matters.
Faith Does Not Require Proof, But It Is Not Blind Either

One of the most important things to understand about faith is that it exists beyond what can be fully proven — but this does not mean it is foolish or irrational.

Faith is not the same as having evidence. A scientist who measures and confirms a result "knows" something. The person who trusts their doctor without fully understanding the medicine believes on faith — based on experience, reputation, and reasonable judgment, but not on personal proof.

At the same time, faith is not the same as wishful thinking or believing something for no reason at all. Healthy faith is usually built on a foundation: past experiences, the character of the person trusted, or the consistency of what you have observed. The leap of faith is not a leap into the dark — it is a step beyond the last visible foothold, based on your confidence in the ground that brought you this far.

So when someone says "I have faith in you," they are not saying "I have mathematically proven you are reliable." They are saying: "Based on what I know and feel, I trust you deeply and I am willing to depend on you."

In everyday life, faith is used widely, beyond religious settings.

You can have faith in a person — a parent, a friend, a leader — meaning you trust their character, their intentions, or their ability. "I have complete faith in her" means you believe she will come through, even if you can't guarantee it.

You can have faith in an idea or system — faith in democracy, faith in science, faith in justice. Here, faith means a deep confidence that the idea is sound and worth committing to, even when individual results are imperfect or uncertain.

You can have faith in the future — a belief that things will work out, that progress is real, that good will eventually win. This kind of faith sustains people through difficulty. It is not naive — it is a choice to trust the larger arc of events.

In religious life, faith takes on its deepest and most specific meaning. Here, faith refers to belief in God, a divine power, or the teachings of a religion — held without scientific proof of God's existence, but with sincere personal conviction and often with spiritual experience.

Religious faith is not just agreeing to a set of facts ("Yes, I believe God exists"). It is a living, personal relationship with the divine — one that shapes how a person lives, what they value, and how they face suffering and death. It is an orientation of the whole person toward something larger than themselves.

The word is also used to refer to an entire religion as a system: "the Christian faith," "the Islamic faith," "the Jewish faith." Here, faith means the whole body of beliefs, practices, and community that a religion encompasses.

A few important expressions built around the word faith will help round out your understanding:

In good faith means acting with honest, sincere intentions — without trying to deceive or manipulate. If you enter a negotiation "in good faith," you are genuinely trying to reach a fair agreement, not playing tricks. Its opposite, bad faith, means pretending to cooperate while actually intending to deceive.

To keep faith (with someone) means to remain loyal and true to your promises or commitments. "She kept faith with her team even when things got hard." To break faith means to betray that loyalty or violate a promise.

To take something on faith means to accept it as true without demanding proof. "He told me the plan would work, and I took it on faith." This can be positive (trust) or slightly risky (blind acceptance), depending on context.

A leap of faith is a decision to commit to something despite uncertainty — to move forward based on trust rather than guaranteed outcomes. Starting a business, getting married, or choosing a new path in life can all be described as a leap of faith.
How Faith Differs From Similar Words

Since faith overlaps with several nearby words, it helps to see where the lines are drawn.

Faith vs. belief: Belief is broader and more passive. You can believe something trivial ("I believe it will rain tomorrow") without it mattering much to you. Faith carries weight — it implies personal investment and a willingness to act on what you believe. Faith is belief that commits you.

Faith vs. hope: Hope is a desire for something good to happen — it looks forward with longing. Faith is stronger and more confident — it is a conviction, not just a wish. You hope you'll get the job; you have faith that you will find your way in life.

Faith vs. knowledge: Knowledge is based on proof, direct experience, or logic. Faith exists where knowledge ends. This is not a failure — it is simply a recognition that life constantly asks us to act before we have complete information. Faith fills that gap with trust rather than with paralysis.

Faith vs. certainty: Certainty means no doubt at all. Faith, by its very nature, allows for the possibility of doubt — but chooses to trust anyway. A person of genuine faith is not someone who has never questioned; they are someone who has chosen to hold on despite questions. This is why faith is often considered a virtue — it requires courage.
The Emotional and Moral Weight of Faith

Finally, it is worth noting that faith is considered one of the most important and admired human qualities across nearly all cultures. To be faithful — to be a person of faith — means you are reliable, loyal, and grounded. You don't abandon your commitments when things get uncertain.

Faith gives people the strength to endure hardship, the courage to take risks, and the stability to build long-term relationships and goals. Without faith — of some kind, in something — it is very hard to act at all, because action always involves uncertainty.

In this sense, faith is not just a religious word. It is a fundamentally human one.
5849: Faithless describes someone — or something — that has broken faith. "Breaking faith" means violating the trust, loyalty, or commitment that was expected of them. The word points directly at a betrayal of something that was owed.

Faithless has two closely connected meanings:

The first and most common meaning is: disloyal; not keeping one's promises or commitments. This is the sense you will encounter most often in everyday life. A faithless person was entrusted with loyalty — through a relationship, a duty, a promise, or a role — and chose to betray it. The betrayal can be toward a person, a group, a cause, or a responsibility.

A faithless partner is someone in a romantic relationship who cheats on or betrays their partner. A faithless ally is a friend or partner who abandons you when you count on them the most. A faithless leader is someone in a position of authority who betrays the people they were supposed to serve. Notice the pattern: in every case, someone was given trust, and they broke it.

The second meaning is: without religious faith; not believing in God or religion. This sense is more formal and literary, and you'll find it more often in religious texts, older writing, or poetry than in everyday conversation. "He preached to a faithless generation" means he preached to people who had lost or abandoned their religious belief. This usage carries less of a moral sting than the first — it's closer to a plain description of an absence of belief, though in religious contexts it can still carry disappointment or sadness.

Both meanings share the same root idea: the absence of faith — whether that's faith in a person (loyalty), or faith in God (belief).

"Faithless" is not a neutral word. It carries serious moral weight, especially in its first meaning. When you call someone faithless, you are not simply saying they were forgetful, unreliable, or inconsistent. You are saying they broke a deep, meaningful bond — one they knew they were bound to honour. There is a strong sense of deliberate betrayal in the word. The person knew what loyalty or commitment was expected of them, and they turned away from it anyway.

This makes "faithless" a harsh, heavy word. It is not something you'd say lightly.

The adjective can describe a person ("a faithless friend"), a group or generation ("a faithless people"), an act or quality ("faithless behaviour"), or even abstract things like promises made without any real intention of being kept ("faithless vows"). It can also occasionally describe a thing or institution that has failed in its duty.

There is also a specific legal and political term worth knowing: a faithless elector. In the United States Electoral College system, an elector is a person chosen to cast a formal vote for president. A "faithless elector" is one who votes for a different candidate than the one they pledged to support — they broke their commitment. This is a real, documented usage of the word.

It helps to place "faithless" on a scale:

Unreliable → Disloyal → Faithless → Treacherous

Someone unreliable simply can't be counted on — they might forget, be inconsistent, or fail to follow through, but not necessarily out of any ill intent. Someone disloyal didn't stand by you — they may have put their own interests first or stopped supporting you. Someone faithless violated a genuine, serious bond — a vow, a duty, a heartfelt commitment. They betrayed your trust in a meaningful way. Someone treacherous goes even further — they actively worked to harm you through their betrayal, often with calculation and deception.

"Faithless" sits in the upper range of this scale. It is a serious accusation.

Unfaithful is the closest synonym and is nearly interchangeable, but it is more commonly used in romantic contexts — an unfaithful spouse, for example. "Faithless" has a broader, slightly more formal reach and can apply to duties, causes, and beliefs beyond just romance.

Disloyal is similar but somewhat softer. Not everyone who is disloyal has made an explicit, solemn commitment, whereas "faithless" implies that the bond was real and known.

Treacherous is stronger and implies active harm — not just abandoning someone, but working against them.

Perfidious is the most formal and literary equivalent; it means deceitful and habitually untrustworthy, often over a long period of time.

False (as in "a false friend") is a milder, more general term for someone who pretends loyalty while not actually offering it.

The natural opposite of faithless is faithful — loyal, keeping one's promises, and steadfast in commitment. Other opposites include loyal (unwavering in allegiance), trustworthy (reliably keeping commitments), devoted (deeply and sincerely committed), and true (in its literary sense of reliable and honest, as in "a true friend").

To really absorb a word, seeing it used in different contexts is essential:

"She discovered that her faithless friends had shared her secrets the moment she left the room."

"The faithless soldier deserted his post in the middle of the battle, leaving his comrades behind."

"History remembers faithless rulers not for their power, but for their betrayals."

"The old preacher lamented that he lived in a faithless age, when people had turned away from belief."

"He proved faithless to every promise he ever made — his words simply didn't mean anything."

"A faithless ally is worse than no ally at all, because they give you a false sense of security."

If you want to carry just one idea away: faithless means having broken a bond of trust, loyalty, or commitment — or, in its religious sense, having no belief in God. It is a word that judges. It does not merely describe someone who failed; it names them as someone who betrayed something real and meaningful. Use it carefully, because it carries weight.
5850: A fake is something — or someone — that appears to be real, genuine, or authentic, but is not. The essential quality of a fake is this gap between appearance and reality. It looks like the real thing. It may even claim to be the real thing. But it isn't.

For something to be called a fake, two things must be true at the same time:

  1. It is not what it claims or seems to be. It lacks the genuine quality it presents.
  2. It is meant to be mistaken for something real. There is an element of deception — someone is being misled, whether deliberately or not.

Both conditions work together. Something that is honestly labeled as an imitation is not a fake. But something that passes itself off as the real thing — when it isn't — is a fake.

1. Fake Objects

This is the most common use. A fake is a physical thing that has been made to look like something genuine but lacks its true nature, origin, or value.

  • A fake diamond looks like a real diamond but is made of glass or cubic zirconia. It has none of the properties of a real diamond.
  • A fake Rolex watch looks like the branded original but is cheaply manufactured. It uses the brand's appearance without being the genuine product.
  • A fake banknote looks like real money but is counterfeit — it has no legal value and its use is illegal.
  • A fake passport looks like an official document but is forged, meaning it was not issued by any government authority.
  • A fake medicine looks like a real drug but may contain no active ingredient, or a harmful one.

In each case, the object has been designed — whether cleverly or crudely — to deceive someone into believing it is genuine.

2. A Fake Person

When "fake" is used as a noun to describe a person, it means someone who is not what they present themselves to be. They are playing a role, projecting a false identity, or pretending to have qualities, qualifications, or credentials they do not actually possess.

  • A person who claims to be a doctor but has no medical degree is a fake.
  • Someone who pretends to be wealthy, educated, or influential — when they are not — is a fake.
  • A person who performs emotions or friendship insincerely, purely to gain something, is called a fake in everyday speech.

Calling someone a fake is a serious accusation. It means their public self is a performance — a constructed illusion designed to manipulate how others see them.

3. A Fake in Art and Documents (Forgery)

In the world of art, literature, and historical documents, a fake is specifically called a forgery — but the noun "fake" covers this meaning too.

  • A fake Picasso painting is one that was made by someone else but presented as Picasso's own work.
  • A fake letter is a document created to look like it was written by someone famous, to deceive collectors or historians.
  • A fake signature on a contract or artwork is one that was forged — written to imitate someone's genuine signature.

Here, the deception is often very deliberate and can have serious legal consequences.
How a Fake Differs from Similar Words

These words are closely related to "fake," but they are not the same:

Fake vs. Copy / Replica:
A copy or replica is an honest reproduction. A museum sells a replica of an ancient statue in its gift shop, and everyone knows it is a replica. No one is being deceived. A fake, by contrast, is a copy or imitation that is passed off as the real thing. The deception is what makes it a fake.

Fake vs. Imitation:
An imitation is something made to resemble another thing. The word itself is neutral — it doesn't necessarily imply fraud. "Imitation leather" on a product label is honest; the buyer knows it isn't real leather. But if that same product were sold as genuine leather, it would become a fake.

Fake vs. Mistake:
A mistake is accidental. A fake is (usually) deliberate — it involves an intention to deceive. If a seller genuinely believed a painting was authentic and sold it in good faith, the painting might still be a fake, but the seller did not knowingly deal in fakes.

Intent is an important, but complicated, part of what makes something a fake.

When we call an object a fake, we are making a statement about what it is, regardless of who made it or why. A counterfeit coin is a fake coin, even if the person who made it had died a hundred years ago.

When we call a person a fake, however, intent is central. We are saying that they knowingly misrepresent themselves. It is a moral judgment — not just a factual description.
The Sense of Fraud and Harm

A fake is not a neutral word. It carries a strong negative meaning because fakes cause harm:

  • A fake medicine can harm a patient who believes they are receiving real treatment.
  • A fake expert can give dangerous advice.
  • A fake banknote defrauds the person who accepts it.
  • A fake friend can emotionally harm someone who trusted them.

This is why discovering that something is a fake is almost always a moment of betrayal — the discovery that trust was misplaced, that what seemed reliable was actually hollow.

Over time, "fake" has expanded in everyday language beyond strict fraud:

  • "That smile is a total fake" — the smile is forced; the emotion behind it is not genuine.
  • "He's such a fake" — said about someone who changes their personality depending on who is watching, performing rather than being themselves.
  • "The whole thing was a fake" — the entire situation, event, or encounter was staged or engineered to create a false impression.

In these uses, the word captures something more than just fraud — it captures inauthenticity, the absence of genuine feeling, genuine identity, or genuine reality.

A fake (noun) is anything — object, person, document, or situation — that is not what it appears or claims to be, and that creates a false impression of being genuine. The word implies deception, a gap between the surface and the truth, and often a betrayal of trust. What distinguishes a fake from a simple copy or imitation is precisely this: it is designed, or at least functions, to make you believe it is real when it is not.
5851:
Before you can understand the full idiom, you need to understand the word facade (sometimes spelled façade).

In its literal sense, a facade is the front wall or face of a building — what you see when you stand outside and look at it. Here's the key thing: a building's facade can look grand, polished, and beautiful on the outside, while the inside is completely different — maybe old, broken down, or under construction.

Think of a movie set. The buildings look real and impressive from the front. But if you walk around the back, there's nothing — just wooden planks holding up a painted surface. That "front" is a facade.

Now, in everyday language, "facade" is used to describe a false or misleading outward appearance that a person puts on to hide what's really going on inside — their true feelings, true character, or true situation.
So What Does "Fake a Facade" Mean?

To "fake a facade" means to deliberately and consciously put on a false front — to project an image of yourself to the outside world that does not match your inner reality.

When someone fakes a facade, they are essentially wearing an emotional or social mask. They want others to see them a certain way, so they carefully craft and maintain that image — even though it is not authentic.

In the simplest terms: you appear one way on the outside while feeling or being something completely different on the inside.
Why Do People Say "Fake a Facade" Instead of Just "Put on a Facade"?

Great question. A facade is already, by definition, something false. So why add the word "fake" to it?

The word "fake" in this idiom adds an extra layer of intention and effort. It emphasizes that the person is not accidentally coming across differently — they are actively working to construct and maintain that false front. It highlights the calculated, deliberate nature of the deception.

So:

  • "He has a facade" → he appears differently than he is.
  • "He faked a facade" → he consciously and skillfully constructed a false front.

The idiom carries a sense of strategy and effort behind the deception.
Everyday Examples to Make It Crystal Clear

Example 1 — Emotions:
Sarah just went through a painful breakup. But at work the next day, she smiles, laughs, and tells everyone she's doing great. She is faking a facade of happiness and confidence while she is hurting deeply inside.

Example 2 — Financial status:
Mark is in serious debt. But he drives an expensive car he can barely afford, wears designer clothes, and talks about his "investments." He is faking a facade of wealth to impress those around him.

Example 3 — Confidence:
A student is terrified before giving a speech. But she walks to the front of the class with a straight posture, a steady voice, and a calm smile. She is faking a facade of confidence even though her hands are trembling inside.

Example 4 — Happiness in a relationship:
A couple tells friends and family that everything is perfect between them, when in reality they argue constantly at home. They are faking a facade of a happy relationship.
The Core Idea in One Sentence
Faking a facade = showing the world a carefully constructed version of yourself that hides the truth of what you actually feel, think, or are.
What Kind of Things Can a Facade Hide?

People fake facades to cover up many things, including:

  • Pain or sadness (pretending to be happy)
  • Fear or insecurity (pretending to be confident)
  • Weakness (pretending to be strong)
  • Financial struggle (pretending to be wealthy)
  • A troubled relationship or life (pretending everything is perfect)
  • Moral or ethical failings (pretending to be honest or virtuous)
  • Loneliness (pretending to be social and satisfied)
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom almost always carries a negative or critical tone. When you say someone is "faking a facade," you are implying:

  • They are being dishonest — with others, or even with themselves.
  • There is something they feel ashamed of, afraid of, or vulnerable about.
  • The image they show the world is not who they truly are.

However, it's worth noting that faking a facade isn't always purely selfish or evil. Sometimes people do it out of self-protection, to survive difficult environments, or because society pressures them to appear a certain way. That doesn't make it right, but it makes it deeply human.
Where Does This Come From? (Origin and Background)

The word "facade" entered English from French, where it means "face" or "front." It is rooted in the Italian word facciata and ultimately the Latin word facies, meaning "face" or "appearance."

The architectural meaning — the front of a building — came first. Over time, people began using it metaphorically to describe the "front" that a person shows to the world. This figurative use became extremely common in literature, psychology, and everyday speech. Sigmund Freud and later psychologists used similar concepts to describe how people construct social personas to hide their inner lives.

The full phrase "fake a facade" developed naturally from this figurative use, emphasizing the active and intentional construction of that false front.
Similar Expressions (So You Can Recognize the Same Idea Elsewhere)

You will often encounter related phrases in English that carry the same or very similar meaning:

  • "Put up a facade" — the most common version; to construct a false front.
  • "Wear a mask" — to hide your true self behind a false identity.
  • "Keep up appearances" — to maintain a certain outward image for social reasons.
  • "Play pretend" — more childlike, but used for adults too when they are being insincere.
  • "Put on an act" — to perform a role that isn't genuinely you.
  • "Two-faced" — a person who shows one face publicly and another privately (though this leans more toward hypocrisy).
  • "Smoke and mirrors" — using illusions to hide the truth.

All of these share the same central theme: the gap between appearance and reality.
A Quick Way to Always Remember This Idiom

Think of a movie set.

The buildings look gorgeous and real from the camera's angle. But the moment the camera turns, you see it's all hollow — just painted wood. The set designers faked a facade of a real city. When people do this in life, they are doing the exact same thing — building a beautiful, impressive front that has nothing solid behind it.
Summary

ConceptMeaning
  • Facade = a false outward appearance, like the front of a building that hides what's inside.
  • Fake a facade = to deliberately and consciously construct and maintain that false outward appearance.
  • Why people do it = to hide pain, fear, weakness, shame, or any truth they don't want the world to see.
  • Tone = critical and negative; implies inauthenticity.
  • Key feeling = the gap between who you appear to be and who you actually are.

That's everything you need to know about this idiom — the word behind it, the meaning, the emotional weight, the origin, the usage, and how it compares to similar expressions. You now have a complete, lasting understanding of "fake a facade."
5852: Falafel is a popular Middle Eastern food. It refers to small, round or slightly flattened balls (or sometimes patties) that are deep-fried until crispy on the outside.---

Falafel is made from chickpeas (sometimes fava beans, or a mix of both). The dried chickpeas are soaked in water overnight to soften them, but — importantly — they are never cooked before being ground. This raw, soaked chickpea paste is then blended with fresh herbs like parsley and cilantro, along with garlic, onion, and spices such as cumin and coriander. A small amount of flour or baking soda is often added to hold everything together and make the balls light and slightly airy inside.

The mixture is shaped into golf ball–sized rounds or small patties, and then deep-fried in oil until the outside turns a deep golden-brown or dark brown.
What it looks, feels, and tastes like

From the outside, falafel has a crispy, crunchy crust with a dark brownish colour. On the inside, it is soft, slightly dense, and green-tinged — that green colour comes from all the fresh herbs mixed in.

The taste is savory, earthy, and herby, with the warm depth of cumin and coriander coming through. It is quite filling because chickpeas are protein-rich and starchy.

Falafel is a very versatile food. The most common way to eat it is stuffed inside a pita bread (a soft, round flatbread with a pocket), along with fresh vegetables like tomato, cucumber, and lettuce, pickled vegetables, and sauces — most commonly tahini sauce (made from sesame paste) or hummus (a dip made from chickpeas). This whole combination is often called a "falafel wrap" or "falafel pita."

It is also served:

  • On a plate as a snack or starter, often with dipping sauces on the side
  • As part of a mezze spread — a Middle Eastern-style meal where many small dishes are served together at once
  • Over rice or salad

The word "falafel" can refer to:

  • A single piece: "I dropped a falafel on my shirt."
  • Several pieces or a portion: "She ordered a plate of falafel."
  • The dish as a concept: "Falafel is one of my favourite street foods."

The plural can be either "falafels" or simply "falafel" — both are widely accepted.
Where it comes from and its cultural importance

Falafel is a staple street food across the Middle East, especially in countries like Egypt, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, and Syria. It has been eaten in this region for centuries. Today, it is eaten all over the world and is especially popular as a vegetarian and vegan option, since it contains no meat or animal products.

In many Middle Eastern cities, small falafel shops called falafel stands serve it fresh and hot from the fryer, wrapped quickly in pita, and handed to customers on the go — much like how a fast-food burger works in the West. It is cheap, filling, and deeply beloved.

In short: falafel is a crispy, herb-filled, deep-fried chickpea ball or patty — a classic Middle Eastern street food, eaten in pita bread with vegetables and sauce, and loved worldwide for its bold flavour and satisfying texture.
5853: A falcon is a bird of prey — meaning a bird that hunts and kills other animals for food. It belongs to a specific group of hunting birds, and while people sometimes use words like "hawk," "eagle," and "falcon" interchangeably in casual talk, a falcon is its own distinct kind of bird with unique features that set it apart.
What Does a Falcon Look Like?

Falcons are built for speed in the air. A few physical traits make them instantly recognizable:

  • Pointed, swept-back wings. Unlike hawks and eagles, whose wings are broad and rounded, a falcon's wings are long, narrow, and taper to a sharp point — almost like the wings of a fighter jet. This shape allows them to cut through the air with minimal resistance.
  • A compact, streamlined body. Falcons are not bulky. They are lean and aerodynamic.
  • A notched beak. Falcons have a small, tooth-like notch on their upper beak (called a tomial tooth). No other birds of prey have this. They use it to snap the neck of their prey quickly and efficiently.
  • A "moustache" marking. Many falcons have a dark stripe or patch running downward from below the eye — almost like a moustache. This is a useful identification clue.
  • Dark eyes in most species, giving them an intense, focused appearance.

Falcons range in size. The smallest, like the American Kestrel, are roughly the size of a pigeon. The largest, like the Gyrfalcon, can be over half a meter long.

This is where falcons truly stand apart. They are aerial hunters — they catch their prey in the open sky, not in forests or on the ground.

Their signature hunting move is called a stoop — a high-speed, near-vertical dive from high altitude directly at their target. During this dive, a falcon tucks its wings close to its body and plummets downward with extraordinary precision.

The Peregrine Falcon is the most famous example. During a stoop, it can reach speeds of over 320 km/h (200 mph), making it the fastest animal on Earth — faster than any land animal, fish, or other bird. No other creature moves faster under its own power.

When a falcon strikes prey, it uses its notched beak to deliver a precise bite to the back of the neck, severing the spine. This is different from eagles and hawks, which kill primarily by gripping and crushing with their powerful talons.

Most falcons eat birds that they catch in mid-air. Larger falcons can take birds as big as ducks and pigeons. Smaller falcons eat insects, bats, lizards, and small mammals. Some falcons are highly specialized — for example, the Bat Falcon of the Americas hunts almost exclusively bats and large insects at dusk.

Falcons are found on every continent except Antarctica — which makes them one of the most widespread groups of birds on the planet. Different species have adapted to radically different environments: open grasslands, mountains, deserts, coastlines, Arctic tundra, and even cities (Peregrine Falcons famously nest on the ledges of tall buildings in cities like New York, London, and Mumbai, where they hunt pigeons).

They generally prefer open spaces where they can spot prey from a distance and dive without obstruction. You will rarely find falcons deep inside dense forests — that is more the territory of hawks.
How Are Falcons Different from Hawks and Eagles?

This is a very common point of confusion, and it is worth clearing up:

  • Hawks have broader, rounder wings, designed for maneuvering through trees. They tend to hunt by ambush in wooded areas and kill mostly with their talons. Hawks and falcons are not closely related despite both being "birds of prey."
  • Eagles are generally much larger than falcons, with massive broad wings designed for soaring on air currents. Many eagles eat fish or scavenge carrion (dead animals). Eagles and hawks are close relatives, but falcons belong to a different evolutionary lineage entirely.
  • Owls hunt at night (most are nocturnal), have forward-facing eyes for depth perception in darkness, and are in a completely different group from falcons.

In fact, scientifically speaking, falcons are more closely related to parrots than they are to hawks or eagles — though this is a fact that surprises most people.

• Peregrine Falcon — The most well-known, found worldwide, fastest animal on Earth.
  • Gyrfalcon — The largest falcon, found in the Arctic; historically prized by royalty.
  • American Kestrel — The smallest falcon in North America; often seen hovering over roadsides.
  • Merlin — A small, fast falcon that specializes in catching small birds.
  • Saker Falcon — A large falcon of open steppes and deserts in Asia and Eastern Europe.
  • Hobby — A graceful, swift falcon known for catching dragonflies and swifts in mid-air.
  • Lanner Falcon — Common in Africa and parts of southern Europe.

Humans have had a special relationship with falcons for thousands of years through a practice called falconry — the art of training falcons (and some hawks) to hunt prey for their human handler. A person who practices this is called a falconer.

In falconry, a falcon is trained to fly free, hunt, and return to the falconer's gloved hand. This requires enormous patience and skill, and builds a genuine bond between bird and human. Falconry is one of the oldest partnerships between humans and animals, practiced for at least 4,000 years, and it is still alive today as both a sport and a cultural tradition in many parts of the world, particularly in the Middle East, Central Asia, and Europe.

In the Arab world especially, the falcon — particularly the Saker and Peregrine — holds deep cultural and national significance. It is a symbol of power, freedom, and noble heritage.

Because of their speed, sharp vision, and fierce hunting ability, falcons have long been symbols of power, precision, freedom, and nobility across many cultures. Ancient Egyptians worshipped the falcon-headed god Horus. Falcons appear on national emblems, flags, and crests across the Middle East and elsewhere. The word "falcon" is also a popular name for military aircraft, sports teams, and more.

A falcon is a lean, pointed-winged bird of prey, built for high-speed aerial hunting. It kills with a precise bite from its notched beak rather than with its talons. Found worldwide, it is the undisputed speed champion of the animal kingdom. It is neither a hawk nor an eagle, though it resembles them at a glance. Humans have hunted alongside falcons for millennia, and these birds carry deep symbolic weight in many cultures as emblems of speed, freedom, and sharpness of purpose.
5854:
Before anything else, picture something made of many pieces held together — like a sandwich, a building, or a friendship. Now imagine those pieces slowly separating until nothing holds them together anymore. That image is the heart of "fall apart."

"Fall apart" is a phrasal verb (a verb + a preposition that together carry a special meaning). It describes the process of something breaking down, collapsing, or completely losing its structure — either physically or in a more emotional/abstract sense.

It is always used without an object. This means something falls apart on its own. You cannot "fall apart" something else. You say "The plan fell apart," never "He fell apart the plan."
Meaning 1: Physical Breaking (Literal)

This is the most straightforward meaning. When a physical object breaks into pieces or disintegrates, it falls apart.

This usually implies the object has become so old, weak, or damaged that it can no longer hold its shape.

Examples:

  • "The old paperback book was so worn out that it literally fell apart when I opened it."
  • "Don't wash that jacket too many times — it'll fall apart."
  • "The ancient temple had fallen apart over centuries of neglect."

Key feeling: Something that was once whole is now in pieces. The breakdown happens because the thing could no longer hold itself together.
Meaning 2: A Plan, Deal, or Situation Collapses (Figurative)

This is one of the most common uses. When a plan, agreement, project, or arrangement stops working and fails completely, we say it "fell apart."

Unlike something that was carefully shut down or ended on purpose, when something falls apart, it collapses on its own, often unexpectedly or due to problems from within.

Examples:

  • "They worked on the business deal for months, but it fell apart at the last minute."
  • "The peace talks fell apart because neither side was willing to compromise."
  • "My travel plans fell apart when the airline cancelled all its flights."
  • "The whole project fell apart after the team leader quit."

Key feeling: Failure that happens by itself — not planned, not graceful. Something that should have worked simply did not hold together.
Meaning 3: A Relationship or Group Breaks Down (Figurative)

When a relationship (friendship, marriage, family bond) or a group (a team, a company, a community) stops functioning and breaks down, it falls apart.

Again, this usually happens gradually, due to internal problems — not because someone decided to end it cleanly.

Examples:

  • "Their friendship fell apart after a serious misunderstanding that was never resolved."
  • "The band fell apart due to creative differences among the members."
  • "Many families fall apart when they stop communicating honestly with each other."
  • "The company started falling apart once it lost its most talented employees."

Key feeling: Something that once had connection and unity has now lost it. The bond that held people together has weakened and broken.
Meaning 4: A Person Loses Emotional Control (Figurative)

When a person is hit by extreme grief, stress, or shock and can no longer keep their emotions under control, we say they "fall apart."

This describes a state where someone becomes so overwhelmed that they break down — often crying, shaking, or simply becoming unable to function normally.

Examples:

  • "She completely fell apart when she heard that her father had passed away."
  • "He tried to stay strong at the funeral, but he fell apart during the speech."
  • "I could see she was about to fall apart — her hands were shaking and her eyes were filled with tears."
  • "After months of pressure, he finally fell apart and had to take a break from work."

Key feeling: The emotional self — which a person normally keeps composed — can no longer hold together. This is deeply human and is not a criticism; it simply describes being overwhelmed.
Meaning 5: Something Gradually Deteriorates (Figurative)

When a place, system, or situation slowly gets worse over time until it is no longer functioning well, we say it is falling apart. This meaning focuses on slow, progressive decline.

Examples:

  • "The neighborhood fell apart after the main factory closed and people lost their jobs."
  • "The country's infrastructure is falling apart — roads are cracked, and bridges are unsafe."
  • "Without proper maintenance, even the best systems will fall apart over time."

Key feeling: A slow, sad decay — the way something once strong becomes weak and broken through neglect or misfortune.
Tense and Forms

Since "fall apart" is a phrasal verb, here is how it changes across tenses:

  • Present: "The situation is falling apart."
  • Past: "The deal fell apart."
  • Perfect: "Everything has fallen apart."
  • Future: "If we don't act now, this will fall apart."
  • Continuous: "I can see this plan is falling apart."
Register and Tone

"Fall apart" is informal to neutral in tone. It fits comfortably in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • News articles
  • Novels and storytelling
  • Emotional discussions

It is not too casual (like slang) and not too formal (like legal language), which means you can use it in a wide variety of situations without sounding out of place.
A Useful Variation: "Falling Apart at the Seams"

A popular extended version of this idiom is "falling apart at the seams." The "seams" refer to the stitching that holds clothing together. When a garment's seams break, the whole thing unravels.

This version is used to describe something that is visibly breaking down from the inside out, often in a way that feels total and unstoppable.

  • "This old coat is falling apart at the seams." (literal)
  • "The organization is falling apart at the seams — there is chaos in every department." (figurative)
Related Expressions

These expressions carry a similar meaning and are good to know alongside "fall apart":

  • Break down — often used for machines, systems, or people under stress. ("The car broke down." / "He broke down in tears.")
  • Collapse — a sudden, dramatic failing. ("The company collapsed overnight.")
  • Crumble — gradual breaking into pieces, often used for structures, empires, or resolve. ("The empire crumbled over decades.")
  • Come apart — very close in meaning to "fall apart"; slightly more informal. ("The deal came apart.")
  • Unravel — when something carefully woven or planned begins to loosen and fail. ("The whole conspiracy began to unravel.")
  • Go to pieces — used almost exclusively for a person losing emotional control. ("She went to pieces at the news.")
  • Fall to pieces — a close synonym; slightly more dramatic in tone. ("He fell to pieces after the breakup.")
Quick Summary of All Meanings

• Physical object → breaks apart into pieces.
  • Plan or deal → collapses and fails to succeed.
  • Relationship or group → loses its bond and breaks down.
  • A person emotionally → loses control and breaks down in grief or stress.
  • A place or system over time → deteriorates and stops functioning well.

In every single case, the central idea is the same: something that once held together no longer can.
5855:
To fall back on something means to use it as a backup or a last resort when your main option has failed, run out, or isn't available. You rely on it because you have no better choice at that moment.

Think of it this way: you're walking forward, your path gets blocked, and so you fall back — you retreat — and land on something safe behind you. That safe thing underneath you is what you're "falling back on." It catches you.

"He lost his job, so he fell back on his savings to pay rent."

Here, his savings were not his first choice for paying rent — his salary was. But when his salary disappeared, he had to retreat and use his savings as a backup. He fell back on them.
What Kind of Things Can You "Fall Back On"?

You can fall back on almost anything that acts as a backup resource — money, skills, people, plans, or habits.

Money or resources:

"When the business failed, she fell back on her inheritance."

A skill or talent:

"He couldn't find work as an actor, so he fell back on his cooking skills and got a job at a restaurant."

A person or relationship:

"She had no one to fall back on when things got hard."

A plan:

"If the first strategy doesn't work, we can always fall back on the original plan."

A habit or behavior:

"Under pressure, he fell back on old habits and started smoking again."
The Very Common Expression: "Have Something to Fall Back On"

This is one of the most frequent ways this phrase appears. It means to have a backup plan or skill ready just in case things go wrong.

"Even if you love painting, study a second subject so you have something to fall back on."

"She trained as a nurse while pursuing her music career, so she'd always have something to fall back on."

Here, the person isn't currently using the backup — they're just making sure it exists if they ever need it. It's about being prepared for the worst.

"Fall back on" has a subtle but important emotional tone. It suggests:

Necessity over preference. You use it because you have to, not because it was your first wish. There's a mild sense of things not going perfectly to plan.

Relief and safety. At the same time, having something to fall back on feels like a safety net — it's a good thing to have. The phrase isn't negative; it's actually often used to encourage people to build backups.

A retreat, not a failure. Falling back isn't the same as giving up. It's a strategic move to something reliable when the main path closes.

The phrase always follows this pattern:

Subject + fall back on + [the backup thing]

The verb changes with tense, as normal:

  • He falls back on his charm whenever he's in trouble. (present)
  • She fell back on her training. (past)
  • We have always fallen back on each other. (present perfect)
  • You can always fall back on this skill. (future/modal)

"Fall back on" always needs an object — the thing being relied upon. You cannot just say "he fell back on" and stop there. You must say what he fell back on.

Don't confuse "fall back on" with:

"Fall back" alone, which simply means to retreat or move backward (used in military or physical contexts). "The soldiers were ordered to fall back." There's no backup resource involved here.

"Fall for" — to be tricked by something, or to develop romantic feelings. Completely different.

"Fall on" — to physically land on something, or to be someone's responsibility. "The duty fell on her shoulders." No backup meaning here.
How It Differs From Similar Phrases

"Resort to" is very close in meaning — it also means to use something as a last option. But "resort to" often sounds slightly more negative or desperate, and is frequently used for actions rather than resources. "He resorted to lying." You wouldn't naturally say "he fell back on lying" — though you could say "he fell back on old tricks."

"Rely on" means to depend on something regularly. It doesn't carry the "backup" or "last resort" idea. You rely on your alarm clock every morning — that's your primary tool. But you fall back on a backup alarm only when the main one fails.

"Turn to" means to seek help or start using something. It's softer and doesn't always imply failure of a first option. "She turned to her friend for advice" just means she went to her friend — there's no abandoned Plan A. But "she fell back on her friend" implies other options were exhausted first.
One Last Way to Remember It

Picture a tightrope walker. They're moving forward with confidence. Suddenly, they lose balance. They fall back — and beneath them is a safety net. That net is what they "fall back on." They didn't plan to use it. They hoped they wouldn't need it. But it's there, it catches them, and it saves them.

That safety net — whether it's money, a skill, a person, or a plan — is always what you "fall back on."
5856: To "fall between two stools" means to fail because you tried to be two things at once, or aim for two goals at once, and ended up achieving neither.

Before understanding the idiom, picture this:

Imagine two wooden stools placed a little apart from each other. Someone tries to sit on both stools at the same time — one foot on one stool, the other foot on the other. What happens? They lose their balance and fall into the gap between the two stools.

That physical image — falling into the empty space between two things — is exactly what this idiom describes, but in a non-physical, everyday-life sense.
What It Really Means (The Two Closely Related Senses)

This idiom is used in two closely connected ways. Both come from the same core idea.

Sense 1: Trying to Do Two Things and Failing at Both

When someone tries to achieve two different goals at the same time, but because they are pulled in two directions, they end up doing neither well — they "fall between two stools."

The key idea here is that the attempt to do both is what causes the failure. If they had focused on just one, they might have succeeded. But by splitting their attention and effort, they fell into the gap.

Examples:

  • A writer tries to make her novel both a serious, deep literary masterpiece and a light, fun beach read. She tries so hard to be both that the book ends up being neither truly deep nor truly fun. Her novel falls between two stools.
  • A restaurant tries to be both a cheap fast-food joint and a fancy fine-dining experience. The food isn't cheap enough for budget customers, and it isn't elegant enough for fine-dining customers. It falls between two stools and loses both types of customers.
  • A student preparing for two exams on the same day splits his time equally between both. He doesn't study enough for either one and fails both. His preparation fell between two stools.

Sense 2: Not Fitting Into Either of Two Categories

This sense is slightly different. Here, something (or someone) ends up in an awkward middle ground — it doesn't clearly belong to one group or the other. It is too much of one thing to be the second, and too much of the second thing to be the first. So it sits uncomfortably between both and fits into neither.

The "failure" here is not always the person's fault — sometimes it's just an awkward situation of being in-between.

Examples:

  • A book is too long and complex to be a children's book, but too simple and short to be a proper adult novel. It falls between two stools — publishers don't know which shelf to put it on.
  • A person applies for a job. They have some experience — more than a complete beginner, but far less than a senior professional. They are too experienced for the entry-level job but too inexperienced for the senior job. They fall between two stools and get neither.
  • A new movie tries to be both a documentary and a fictional drama. It ends up being not realistic enough for documentary fans and not entertaining enough for drama fans. It falls between two stools.

How Sense 1 and Sense 2 Connect

Both senses share the same soul: there are two clear positions/goals, you are caught in the middle, and you end up with nothing. In Sense 1, you actively tried to be both. In Sense 2, you ended up in between without necessarily intending to. In real usage, the two senses often blur together.

This idiom is very old — it goes back to at least the 14th century, making it one of the older idioms in the English language.

The earliest known written record in English is from the poet John Gower, who in 1390 wrote something that translates roughly to: "Between two stools my drunk man falls." Similar expressions existed in Latin and French even earlier, which tells us this was a common idea across cultures in medieval Europe.

In those times, stools (simple seats with no back) were the most common form of seating. People sitting down to eat or rest would use stools constantly. The image of someone clumsily trying to sit on two stools and falling would have been instantly funny and relatable to everyone who heard it — much like how we today might say someone "dropped the ball."

The idiom has survived for over 600 years and is still widely used today in British English in particular, though it is understood across all English-speaking regions.
How to Use It in a Sentence (Grammar Notes)

The idiom is a verb phrase. The verb "fall" changes depending on tense and subject, just like any regular verb. The rest of the phrase — "between two stools" — stays the same.

TenseExample
  • Present: "The project falls between two stools — it's not academic enough for researchers and not practical enough for businesses."
  • Past: "The campaign fell between two stools and failed to attract any clear audience."
  • Future: "If you try to please both groups, the plan will fall between two stools."
  • Present Perfect: "Their strategy has fallen between two stools once again."
  • Continuous/Participle: "The policy is in danger of falling between two stools if it isn't focused soon."

You can also use it about people, things, plans, projects, policies, books, films, or basically anything that can fail by being caught between two goals or categories.
The Tone and Register — When Is It Used?

This idiom is:

  • Neutral to slightly formal — it doesn't sound rude or very casual. It is perfectly fine in professional writing, academic essays, journalism, business meetings, and everyday conversation.
  • Mostly British in origin and frequency, but widely understood globally.
  • Often used when giving criticism or analysis — pointing out why something failed or is likely to fail.
  • Useful when you want to express a nuanced idea elegantly in just a few words. Instead of saying "They tried to do two things at once and ended up doing neither well," you simply say "It fell between two stools."
Similar Idioms — and How They Differ

Understanding related idioms helps you sharpen your understanding of this one.

1. "Jack of all trades, master of none"
This means someone who can do many things but is not excellent at any of them. The focus is on having too many skills spread thin, not just two. "Fall between two stools" is specifically about two things and often refers to a project or plan, not just a person's skills.

2. "Sit on the fence"
This means refusing to take a clear side or make a decision — being deliberately neutral. It's about indecision or cowardice. "Fall between two stools" is different — the person or thing does make an attempt, they just can't commit fully to either side and therefore fail. One is about avoiding a choice; the other is about failing despite (or because of) attempting both.

3. "Between a rock and a hard place"
This means being stuck between two bad or difficult options with no good way out. The focus is on difficulty and being trapped. "Fall between two stools" is about failing by not committing to either of two options — the options aren't necessarily bad, but the in-between position is.

4. "Two birds, one stone"
This is almost the opposite in spirit — it means achieving two goals with one action, successfully. "Fall between two stools" is what happens when the attempt to hit two birds at once goes wrong.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you want to lock the meaning into your memory forever, remember this one sentence:

You aimed for two things. You got neither. You fell between the two stools.

That's it. Any time something (a plan, a product, a person's effort, a piece of writing, a strategy) tries to serve two masters and ends up serving none — that thing has fallen between two stools.
Quick Real-World Scenarios to Test Your Understanding

Read each situation and confirm to yourself that you can see why the idiom applies:

  1. A politician tries to appeal to both very conservative voters and very liberal voters by taking no strong stance on anything. Neither group is impressed. → He fell between two stools.
  2. A new phone is designed to be both a luxury premium device and an affordable budget phone. It ends up too expensive for budget buyers and not premium enough for luxury buyers. → It falls between two stools.
  3. A chef tries to cook a dish that is both completely authentic Thai food and also suited to Western tastes, making it neither truly Thai nor truly Western. → The dish falls between two stools.

You now know everything there is to know about this idiom — its meaning in both senses, where it comes from, how old it is, how to use it grammatically, when to use it, how it differs from similar expressions, and how to spot it in real life. You're fully equipped.
5857:
When something or someone falls by the wayside, it means they fail to continue, get abandoned, or don't survive long enough to reach the finish line.

Think of a race with 50 runners. Not everyone finishes. Some get tired, some get injured, some simply stop. Those who drop out before the end — they "fell by the wayside." The ones who made it to the finish line did not.

The idiom captures the idea of something that started but didn't last.

This idiom is ancient. It comes from a famous story in the Bible called the Parable of the Sower (found in Matthew, Mark, and Luke in the New Testament).

In that story, a farmer scatters seeds across his land. Some seeds fall "by the wayside" — meaning on the hard, trampled ground along the edge of a path or road. Because the ground there is too hard for roots to grow, those seeds never sprout. Birds come and eat them. They are wasted — they had potential, but they came to nothing.

The word "wayside" simply means the side of a road or path. It's an old English word (wayside = way + side). In those times, roads were not perfectly defined, and the edges of paths were hard, barren ground — not the kind of soil where things grow.

So the literal image is: a seed that falls in a bad spot and never grows. Over time, this became a metaphor for anything that starts with promise but doesn't survive or succeed.

Today, people use this idiom in a few closely related ways:

1. A plan or goal gets abandoned.
You start something, but life gets in the way, and you stop. The thing is quietly dropped, forgotten, or never finished.

"She planned to learn the guitar, but that idea fell by the wayside after she started her new job."

2. A person doesn't make it through a process.
In competitions, job applications, training programs — many people start, but only some survive each stage. Those who get eliminated fall by the wayside.

"Out of 200 applicants, most fell by the wayside during the interview process."

3. Something loses priority and slowly disappears.
This is very common. You don't actively quit something — you just… stop doing it. It fades away because other things took over.

"His morning exercise habit fell by the wayside during the winter months."

4. Something fails to survive over time.
Businesses, trends, technologies, movements — things that once seemed important but quietly died out.

"Many social media platforms from the early 2000s have fallen by the wayside."
The Tone and Feeling of the Idiom

This idiom almost always carries a slightly sad or regretful tone. There is an unspoken sense of lost potential — whatever fell by the wayside had a chance, but didn't make it.

It is not a dramatic, explosive kind of failure. It's quieter than that. It suggests something that faded, drifted away, or was left behind — not something that blew up spectacularly.

Think of it as the difference between a candle that burns out versus one that gets knocked over and causes a fire. Falling by the wayside is the candle burning out.

Almost anything that involves effort, continuity, or progress over time:

  • Goals and ambitions → "His dream of writing a novel fell by the wayside."
  • Habits and routines → "Her diet fell by the wayside during the holidays."
  • Relationships → "Old friendships often fall by the wayside when people move to different cities."
  • Projects and plans → "The renovation project fell by the wayside due to a lack of funding."
  • People in a competition → "Half the contestants fell by the wayside in the first round."
  • Ideas and trends → "That technology fell by the wayside once smartphones took over."

It doesn't always mean someone is to blame.
Sometimes things fall by the wayside because of circumstances, bad timing, or external pressure — not personal failure. The idiom is neutral enough to cover both situations.

"The charity project fell by the wayside after the main organizer moved abroad." ← No blame, just circumstances.

"He let his health fall by the wayside because he cared too much about work." ← Here, there is a sense of personal neglect.

It implies something that once had momentum.
